- When sentiment is negative (e.g., -1.00) in recent history, model tends to overcorrect downward; adjust forecast upward slightly to avoid excessive sell-off bias.
- Model often underestimates price spikes in early forecast horizon (e.g., 30d) — especially after recent highs — and fails to capture momentum; add 1–2% buffer to forecast if sentiment is neutral or slightly positive.
- If sentiment is consistently 0.00, model exhibits mean-reversion bias — forecast tends to be too low in the short term; increase baseline by 0.5–1.5% to align with recent price action.
- Overshoots after sharp price drops (e.g., 65.00 → 62.00) are common — model rebounds too aggressively; cap forecast rise to 1.5–2.0% above prior low if sentiment is neutral.
- If sentiment is positive (e.g., 0.50 or above), model underreacts to bullish signals — forecast lags 1–3 days behind true trend; shift forecast 0.5–1.0% higher for next 3–5 days to capture sentiment momentum.
- Model consistently underestimates true price in 30d horizon when sentiment is flat — apply 0.8–1.2% upward adjustment to forecast mean if sentiment is 0.00 over last 5–7 days.
